name: Input guardrails on the user turn do not cover the retrieved turn, because indirect injection arrives as data the app itself fetched
symptom: You put a classifier on the user's prompt. The tests pass against hand-written direct jailbreaks. Then the application retrieves a document the attacker controls - a web page, a wiki page, an email, an issue comment, a support ticket - and the injection succeeds through a turn no input filter was ever applied to.
root_cause: Greshake et al.'s framing is that LLM-integrated applications blur the line between data and instructions: the assumption that the user is the one prompting no longer holds. Their indirect prompt injection has the attacker never touch the user interface at all - they write into data the application will later retrieve. A guardrail placed on the user turn is structurally incapable of seeing this, because the malicious text is not in the user turn; it is in a document your retrieval layer placed into the model's context. The attack surface grows with every retrieval source you add.
workaround: Treat retrieved content as untrusted input of the same class as user input, and filter it as such - at ingestion, not only at the prompt boundary. Concretely: (a) screen documents at index time so poisoned content never enters a context; (b) mark or delimit retrieved spans so the model can distinguish them from instructions; (c) if the model has tools, constrain what any single retrieved span can cause, because an agent's damage is bounded by its capabilities rather than by its instructions.
notes: This is the highest-severity record in the safety slice because the mitigation is architectural, not a knob, and the failure is invisible to prompt-level testing. Related risk recorded separately: corpus poisoning, where the attacker does not need to win the user's request, only to get a document retrieved.
